job.style: a passage rich in numbers, dates or measurements

passage: In our science lab, we tested various materials using a standard 10-centimeter bar magnet. We discovered that while iron, nickel, and cobalt are magnetic, materials like copper and aluminum remain unaffected. When we placed the magnet near a pile of iron filings, we observed that the filings clustered densely at the two ends, while the center remained almost bare. We also learned that magnetism is a permanent property, not a temporary charge like static electricity that fades away. To test this, we heated a magnet to 200 degrees Celsius, which actually caused it to lose its magnetic strength rather than gain it. Furthermore, we used a compass to find directions; the needle aligns with the Earth's magnetic field, not the North Star. Finally, we observed that when we brought two magnets together with like poles facing each other, they pushed away with a force of 5 Newtons, proving that repulsion occurs between magnets. Unlike glue, this magnetic force acts through materials like paper or wood. We must store magnets carefully with iron keepers across their poles to maintain their strength for years, as they do not run out of power like a battery.

items.evidence: To test this, we heated a magnet to 200 degrees Celsius, which actually caused it to lose its magnetic strength rather than gain it.
items.q: Meera heats her bar magnet in a flame. What will most likely happen to its pull?
options: It will stay the same forever
It will change only at the poles
items.explain: Heating a magnet damages it, so it loses magnetic strength instead of gaining it.

wrong.why: thinks heat gives a magnet more energy
thinks magnetism cannot be changed by anything
thinks only the poles are affected by heat

items.evidence: When we placed the magnet near a pile of iron filings, we observed that the filings clustered densely at the two ends, while the center remained almost bare.
items.q: Iron filings cover a bar magnet. Which part is picked up the least?
options: The centre, between the two ends
Both ends, where the poles are
Only the end that points north
Every part holds the same amount
items.explain: The force is strongest at the two ends, so the centre holds almost no filings.

wrong.why: thinks the ends are weak and the centre strong
thinks the force is the same everywhere

items.evidence: Unlike glue, this magnetic force acts through materials like paper or wood.
items.q: Which example shows that a magnet does not work like glue?
options: It pulls a pin through a sheet of paper
It lifts an iron nail off the table
It sticks to a steel door tightly
It pulls two iron pins together
items.explain: Glue needs contact, but a magnet's force acts through paper or wood without touching.

wrong.why: picks a sticking example that fits glue too
picks a pulling example that needs touching
picks another contact example that glue could explain

items.evidence: We must store magnets carefully with iron keepers across their poles to maintain their strength for years, as they do not run out of power like a battery.
items.q: Why can a well-kept magnet still work strongly after many years?
options: Its power does not get used up
Its power slowly grows each year
Its power is recharged by the sun
Its power is stored in a battery
items.explain: A magnet does not run out of power like a battery, so a well-kept one stays strong.

wrong.why: thinks magnets lose power, so a lasting one must refill
thinks magnets gain energy over time
thinks magnetism is a charge that needs recharging
